tei:titleStmt.tei:title: מעשה מיץ
Maaseh Metz, a qinah after a crowd panic and deadly crush in the synagogue over Shavuot in Metz (1714)

tei:div.tei:head: Maaseh Metz, a qinah after a crowd panic and deadly crush in the synagogue over Shavuot in Metz (1714)

tei:lg.tei:l: Woe unto us that such a thing has come to pass in our time,
when our ears hear it, our soul is sick,
that the verse has come to pass
“I will cast a faintness into their hearts.
The sound of a driven leaf shall put you to flight.
Fleeing as though from the sword,
they shall fall though none pursues.
[With no one pursuing, they shall stumble over one another as before the sword.]”

tei:div.tei:p:
Because of this our hearts are sick, our eyes are dimmed
because of the desecration of the Sabbath and holy day
and because of prayers suspended,
in the words of the prophet “Who asked that of you” (Isaiah 1:12)
on that holy day of the giving of our holy Torah
and He has chosen us from among every nation and tongue,
had we been deserving we could have rejoiced
on the day of the giving of the Torah,
a sacred occasion.

And now “We have become the butt of our neighbors,
the scorn and derision of those around us,” (Psalms 79:4)
as though the Temple had been destroyed in our time.
And because poor wretched women were killed
our eyes shed streams of water.
Most of these women had just given birth,
alas, and one was pregnant.
For them — rest, for us—sorrow and anguish and sighs.
The day after the festival
the Burial Society men go early to the cemetery,
the six dead women are buried next to each other in a row.

Henceforth, all must examine their conduct,
every man according to his ways,
and with the proper fruit of their deeds,
attesting that the Lord is upright,
a faithful God, never false,
but He, being merciful,
forgave iniquity and would not destroy
and did not give full vent to His fury and wrath,
and said to the angel who was destroying, “Stay your hand!” etc.

May the Master of Compassion grant our request,
the Lord will guard our going and coming to life and peace,
now and for evermore,
And there will be no more breaching and wailing in our streets
among our brethren, the whole house of Israel,
in all their dwelling places,
and let us say Amen.

tei:note.tei:p: See Turniansky 2006a, p. 595, n. 241.
Leviticus 26:36-37 [part], with two changes: the phrase “in the land of their enemies” is left out, and “put you to flight” appears instead of “put them to flight.”
Cf. Lamentations 5:17.
The incident took place on the Shavuot festival, which celebrates the giving of the Torah.
Cf. “who has chosen us from all peoples and raised us above all tongues” (from the blessing over the wine for holidays and Rosh Hashanah; Mahzor Rosh Hashanah 2014, p. 105).
Cf. “These are the set times of the Lord, the sacred occasions” (Leviticus 23:4).
Cf. as if the destruction of the Temple had taken place in his days” (b.Sanhedrin 22a).
Cf. “My eyes shed streams of water” (Psalms 119:136).
The sources cited earlier in Glikl: Memoirs (p. 303, n. 78) confirm these details.

Up to this point, all details of Gliki’s description of the incident (except those relating to her personal experiences) that have parallels in the sources cited in Turniansky 1006a, p. 587, n. 188, are fully corroborated. However, the sources do not mention most of the events related in the text that follows here, from the paragraph beginning “It is true that talk of this incident continues unabated” through the paragraph ending “I, the mother, heard nothing either.”
Cf. b. Berakhot 5a.
Cf. Jeremiah 51:19.
Psalms 91:16.
Cf. Deuteronomy 31:4; the end of this verse — “true and upright is He” — connects to the former mention: “the Lord is upright” (see previous note).
Cf. Psalms 78:38.
Cf. 1 Samuel 14:16.
A common appellation for God in the liturgy (e.g., see “You are a God slow to anger, you are called the Master of Compassion” in the Selichot prayers (Siddur 1016, p. 914).
Cf. “The Lord will guard your going and coming now and for evermore” (Psalms 111:8). The insertion “to life and peace” is a common blessing formulation (see Siddur 1016, p. 631).
Cf. “There is no breaching and no sortie, and no wailing in our streets” (Psalms 144:14).
For “our brethren, the whole house of Israel,” see Mahzor Rosh Hashanah 1014, p. 195. For “in all their dwelling places,” see Siddur 1016, p. 166.
